title: Normal distribution
examples: How do I find the mean if I only know the standard deviation and a probability?
What does the z-score actually tell me about a data point?
Can I use this rule for data that is not normally distributed?

explain.say: Today we learn about the normal distribution curve. This curve shows how data often clusters around the average value. The shape is always a perfect bell shape.

First, we must standardise our data using the z-score. The z-score tells us how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. The formula is z equals the value minus the mean, all divided by the standard deviation.

Next, we use the empirical rule for quick estimates. About sixty-eight percent of data falls within one standard deviation of the mean. Ninety-five percent falls within two standard deviations. Finally, ninety-nine point seven percent falls within three standard deviations.

items: Convert z-score back to raw score

explain.say: To find the raw score from a probability, we use the inverse normal function. This function takes a probability and gives us the corresponding z-score. We then convert that z-score back to the original data scale.

faq.q: What is the z-score really measuring?
faq.a: The z-score measures how far a specific data point is from the mean in terms of standard deviations. It standardises the data so we can compare different sets.
asks: How many standard deviations away is this point?
What does standardising mean for a data point?

faq.q: Does the empirical rule always work?
faq.a: The empirical rule only accurately applies when the data truly follows a normal distribution. If the data is skewed, the rule will give inaccurate estimates.
asks: Is this rule only for bell curves?
When can I use the 68-95-99.7 rule?

faq.q: How do I find the mean if I know the standard deviation and a probability?
faq.a: You must first use the inverse normal function on the given probability to find the z-score. Then, you use the z-score formula rearranged to solve for the mean.
asks: Can I work backwards from a probability?
What if I need to find μ from a tail probability?

faq.q: What is the difference between the z-score and the t-score?
faq.a: The z-score is used when the population standard deviation is known. The t-score is used when the population standard deviation is unknown and must be estimated from the sample.
asks: When do I use t instead of z?
Are they interchangeable in any situation?

faq.q: If the standard deviation is zero, what happens to the z-score?
faq.a: If the standard deviation is zero, all data points are exactly equal to the mean. The z-score calculation would involve division by zero, which is undefined.
asks: Can the standard deviation ever be zero?

facts: The normal distribution is symmetrical around its mean, median, and mode.
The mean, median, and mode are all equal in a perfect normal distribution.
The z-score calculation standardises any normal variable.
The empirical rule provides approximate percentages for data spread.

quiz.say: A test score is normally distributed with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10. What is the z-score for a raw score of 85?
quiz.why: The z-score tells you exactly how many standard deviations 85 is from the mean of 70.

wrong.1: This mistake happens if you forget to divide by the standard deviation, treating the standard deviation as one.
wrong.2: This mistake occurs if you incorrectly subtract the standard deviation from the raw score before dividing.
wrong.3: This mistake suggests multiplying the result by the standard deviation instead of using it as a direct measure.

quiz.say: Using the empirical rule, approximately what percentage of data falls between 80 and 100, given a mean of 90 and a standard deviation of 10?
quiz.why: The range from 80 to 100 represents exactly one standard deviation below and one standard deviation above the mean.

wrong.1: This is tempting because 95 percent covers two standard deviations, but the range given is only one standard deviation wide.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because 99.7 percent covers three standard deviations, which is much wider than the given range.
wrong.3: This mistake might happen if you only consider the area within one standard deviation of the mean, ignoring the other side.

quiz.say: If the probability of a value being less than x is 0.975, what is the approximate value of x, given μ=50 and σ=5?
quiz.why: A cumulative probability of 0.975 corresponds to a z-score of 1.96, which means x is 1.96 times the standard deviation above the mean.

wrong.1: This assumes the probability of 0.975 means the value is exactly at the mean, ignoring the standard deviation.
wrong.2: This mistake might result from incorrectly using the 68 percent rule, which corresponds to a z-score of one.
wrong.3: This is too high, possibly confusing the probability value with the actual data value on the scale.
